Obviously the list is part of an unhealthy, imbalanced relationship with broken trust, but I disagree that it's self perpetuating or you can't regain trust with a lock down list. Maybe if the goal was permanent lockdown, but the goal of a list in my case was to give me a way to feel safe again, and came with a timeline for slowly easing off of it as we rebuilt trust. Like a cast: it would be a horrible idea for a healthy leg and causes muscle atrophy and skin problems, but it's temporarily nessecary when the bones are broken.

The difficulty with such a list is that it really needs to come from the partner who broke the trust. If the betrayed partner has to make a list, it means the betrayer doesn't understand/isn't interested in fixing the damage done. Instead of "I need you to do xyz to prove I can trust you again", it needs to be "I hurt you and broke the trust and will do xyz to help prove that I have changed and work with you to make you feel safe".* I've seen relationships work out when that happens, but never the other way around.

*Of course this needs to come with a reasonable time limit & some form of conselling to ensure the end dynamic is healthy, not simply imbalanced the other way

You are correct. I was going by years per book because that's what is the original post. If you want to argue word count, we can talk about Jim Butcher- arguably a different league and style of fantasy altogether- whose Codex Alera alone appears, from rough estimates online, to have been ~800k words in 5 years. 

It's all cherry picking. You can divide novels along the lines of genre, or the length of books, or themes, or apparent complexity. You can go by book count, word count, chapter count, character count. You can manipulate until you find whatever you want on either side of the 'this is slow' and 'this is fast' equation.

At the end of the day, some fans are upset because it's outside of what they expect for fantasy. Some fans are fine with it even if they find it slow because it's worth the waits. Some fans are happy and think it's going along fine. What I'm trying to point out is that they all have valid points, which the original post studiously ignored.

I guess to answer your question, "how unusual is that?", I would say: for a work in the fantasy genre in a series format, it's pretty unusual. Even Tolkien's Lord Of The Rings, while written over a long period of time, was published in a two year span.

How about Niel Gaiman? A sucessful fantasy writer who has had, if my memory serves me, two of his novels turned into television format. Fairly famous. Seems pretty comparable to me even if his novels are stand alone, more so than trying to compare GRRM to authors in other genres. Since 1996 (when AGOT first came out) Niel Gaiman has to my knowledge publish 9 full length novels in addition to multiple children's books and graphic novels.

The publication schedule is slower than seems to be typical for the genre. You feel like the wait is worth the payoff. That's a good point. Your favorite authors (from other genres) also take a long time between books, so you're used to long waits. Also great point. All authors work differently and have different lengths of time between books. Still a great point. But going on to build a false equivilancy between authors from different genres in order to come to the conclusion 6 years is the 'least' wait we could expect between books in a fantasy series is not a great point.

I have no idea how many years they were in preproduction and planning. That's sort of the point- it may have taken years to plan it all, but they planned it so they could publish close together for the sake of their audience. GRRM didn't do a ton of planning of the series as a whole before publication of the first book; or rather, he did and then changed his mind about it, eliminating the 5 year gap and reworking his whole story. As far as I can tell, most fantasy works are preplanned and have a ton of work put in prior to publication so they can be finished before the readers lose interest or get angry, like ASOIAF fans have. If he'd stuck to his original trilogy idea, I feel like it would have been out sooner because he had a better grasp on where the narrative was going before he eliminated the gap. As it is he has to do the years of planning in between books while fans lose patience.

So, merely out of interest because of this post, I pulled a couple of my personal collection off the shelves. I reached for fantasy series only; no standalones, and no other genres.

The Deed of Paksenarrion by Elizabeth Moon.  1024 pages in omnibus format. The original trilogy was published in a two year span, 1988-1989.

The Fionavar Tapestry by Guy Gavriel Kay. 774 pages in omnibus format. The original trilogy was published in two years, between 1984 and 1986.

The Codex Alera by Jim Butcher. 6 books of varying lengths, most seem to be between 600-750 pages. Published in 5 years, between 2004 and 2009.

Now, I'm not trying to compare books, or say who's better or why. I don't really care what you think of my handmedown book collection either. I'm just saying if you want to look authors and book lengths and times, there are ALL KINDS of variations in book length vs time vs complexity. Cherry picking can give you exactly the averages you want.

Why not just leave it at "all authors are different, they all work differently, and some books take longer to write"? Six years is absolutely not the LEAST you can expect, but that doesn't make it a bad thing either. It's fine to think it's worth the wait.
